title: Deadlock: Two Locks, Opposite Order
oneLiner: Step two threads that take the same two locks in opposite order into a deadlock, see the four conditions that make it possible, and break it with lock ordering or a timeout.
keyTakeaway: A deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and a circular wait. Break any one and deadlock is impossible. The standard fix is a global lock order (every thread takes lock A before lock B), which makes a cycle in the wait-for graph impossible; the fallback is a timeout (Monitor.TryEnter) that gives up, releases what it holds, and retries.
explanation:
Thread 1 transfers money from account A to account B, so it locks A, then B. Thread 2 transfers from B to A, so it locks B, then A. If thread 1 gets A and, before it reaches B, thread 2 gets B, then thread 1 waits for B (held by thread 2) and thread 2 waits for A (held by thread 1). Neither will ever let go, because each releases only after it gets the lock it is waiting for. The program does not crash and uses no CPU; it just stops. That silence is what makes deadlocks painful in production.

Coffman (1971) showed a deadlock requires four conditions together. Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by only one thread. Hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another. No preemption: nobody can take a resource away from the thread holding it. Circular wait: there is a cycle of threads, each waiting for a resource the next one holds. Drawn as a wait-for graph (an edge from T1 to T2 means T1 waits for something T2 holds), a deadlock is exactly a cycle.

The fixes each break one condition. Lock ordering breaks circular wait: if every thread acquires locks in the same global order (by account id, say), a cycle cannot form, because no thread ever waits for a lower-ranked lock while holding a higher one. This is the answer interviewers want first. Timeouts break no preemption in spirit: Monitor.TryEnter(lockB, timeout) returns false instead of waiting forever, so the thread releases lock A, backs off for a random moment and retries. That turns a deadlock into a possible livelock (both threads retrying in lockstep forever) unless the back-off is randomized. Taking every lock you need at once, or never holding one lock while waiting for another, breaks hold and wait.

Dining philosophers is the same problem with five threads in a ring: each philosopher needs the fork on their left and on their right. If all five pick up their left fork at the same moment, everyone waits for a right fork that is someone else's left fork: a cycle of five. Numbering the forks and making each philosopher pick up the lower-numbered fork first is lock ordering again, and it works.

Databases detect deadlocks rather than prevent them: they keep the wait-for graph, look for a cycle, and abort one transaction (a group of database changes that succeed or fail together) as the victim. The graded lesson after this one asks you to write that detector.
